articles.headline: OFAC Designates New Entities in Connection with Iran
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 6, 2026. This action targets individuals and entities involved in activities supporting the Iranian regime.
These designations aim to further restrict the Iranian government's access to financial resources and its ability to engage in destabilizing activities.
The U.S. Treasury continues to apply pressure on Iran through sanctions to address concerns regarding its nuclear program, support for terrorism, and human rights abuses.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Sanctions on Cuba, Targets Cyber and Transnational Criminal Organizations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on November 5, 2026, targeting cyber-related activities and transnational criminal organizations, alongside additional Cuba designations.

These actions include the designation of ten targets, including Cuban elites, a crude oil shipping network, state-owned import and technical-support entities, and China-based suppliers of the regime's military forces.

OFAC also issued a determination paving the way for sanctions on the electronics, manufacturing, marine, and technology sectors of the Cuban economy, signaling a significant escalation of U.S.-Cuba sanctions policy.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran Designations, Updates Listings, and Amends Venezuela GL
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and updates to certain Iran-related listings on November 4, 2026. This action is part of ongoing efforts to counter the Iranian regime's illicit activities.
In addition to the Iran-related actions, OFAC also published an Iran-related alert and issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question.
The amended Venezuela-related General License aims to provide clarity and adjust existing authorizations concerning transactions involving Venezuela.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Iran-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Iran-related General License on October 29, 2026. This amendment aims to refine existing authorizations related to transactions involving Iran.
General Licenses are issued by OFAC to authorize certain categories of transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under sanctions programs.
The specific details of the amendment were not immediately disclosed, but such changes typically aim to clarify scope or adjust permitted activities under the existing sanctions framework.

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities Related to North Korea and Democratic Republic of the Congo
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on October 28, 2026, targeting entities connected to North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).

These designations are part of ongoing efforts to counter illicit activities by North Korea, including its weapons of mass destruction programs, and to address human rights abuses and corruption in the DRC.
The U.S. Treasury continues to utilize its sanctions authorities to promote international security and human rights globally.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks Settles with OFAC for Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-based networking provider, has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to settle nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

OFAC found that between September 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks exported hardware and software to Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), a Russian defense manufacturer majority-owned by a designated entity, Almaz-Antey.

Despite having a sanctions screening process, Extreme Networks failed to identify MMZA as a blocked entity, even when red flags such as MMZA email addresses and delivery locations were present on purchase orders.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Filing Reports
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on October 26, 2026, regarding blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC.
These amendments aim to provide updated guidance and clarity for U.S. persons and financial institutions on their obligations under OFAC regulations.
The FAQs serve as an important resource for compliance professionals to ensure adherence to U.S. sanctions programs.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran Designations, Removes Belarus and North Korea Listings, and Issues New GLs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 21, 2026, while also removing certain Belarus and North Korea designations.
In conjunction with these actions, OFAC issued new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses and amended Frequently Asked Questions.
These actions reflect a dynamic approach to sanctions, adjusting measures based on ongoing assessments of foreign policy and national security objectives.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Protecting American Intellectual Property Act (PAIPA) Designations and Associated General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026.
These designations are accompanied by the issuance of associated General Licenses, which aim to mitigate unintended consequences and provide specific authorizations related to the new sanctions.

PAIPA targets individuals and entities involved in the theft or misappropriation of American intellectual property, underscoring the U.S. commitment to protecting its technological and economic interests.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question on October 16, 2026.
This amendment aims to provide updated guidance and potentially adjust the scope of authorized transactions involving Venezuela.
General Licenses are crucial for navigating the complex Venezuelan sanctions regime, which has seen various adjustments through licenses since the arrest of Nicolás Maduro in January 2026.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Pays $1,529,685 for Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-based networking provider, has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to settle nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

The violations stemmed from the company's Russian subsidiary exporting hardware and software to a blocked Russian defense manufacturer, Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), between September 2018 and March 2022.

OFAC determined the violations were egregious but voluntarily self-disclosed, and the settlement amount reflects mitigating factors including the company's lack of prior OFAC enforcement history and substantial remedial measures.

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Fined $11,662,930 for Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has agreed to an $11,662,930 settlement with OFAC for 475 apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs, including those related to Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

These violations occurred between September 2021 and April 2025 and involved payments routed through blocked banks, poorly prioritized alerts, delayed watchlist updates, and human error on blocked accounts.
The OFAC settlement is part of a larger coordinated enforcement action by the U.S. Treasury Department, which also included penalties from FinCEN and the OCC totaling over $1.21 billion.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Pays $175,015 for Counter Narcotics Sanctions Violations
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, a California-based freight forwarder, has agreed to pay $175,015 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC counter narcotics sanctions and reporting obligations.

The violations occurred when Pegasus arranged for the shipment of a sugar-packet filling machine from a designated Chinese supplier, Youli Technology Development Co., Ltd., which was on the SDN List for narcotics-related activities.
OFAC found that Pegasus demonstrated reckless disregard by failing to properly screen information in its possession and not investigating further after learning the machine had been detained.

articles.headline: Individual Fined $1,427,230 by OFAC
body: An individual has been assessed a civil penalty of $1,427,230 by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on September 10, 2026.
The details of the apparent violations leading to this significant penalty were not immediately released, but OFAC regularly pursues enforcement actions against individuals for sanctions breaches.
This action underscores OFAC's commitment to enforcing U.S. sanctions laws across all sectors and against all responsible parties, whether corporate or individual.

articles.headline: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. Settles for $60,764 Over Iran Sanctions Violations
body: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc., a Wisconsin-based manufacturer, has agreed to pay $60,764 to settle eight apparent violations of the Iranian Transactions and Sanctions Regulations (ITSR).

The violations stemmed from its Italian subsidiary, Dini Argeo S.r.l., indirectly selling weighing equipment to an Iranian client through a Dubai-based distributor between June 2019 and November 2021.
OFAC determined the violations were non-egregious and voluntarily self-disclosed, with the settlement amount reflecting a base penalty of half the aggregate transaction value.

articles.headline: FTI Consulting, Inc. Pays $1,050,000 for Indirect Dealings with Sanctioned Russian Bank
body: FTI Consulting, Inc., a Washington D.C.-based international consulting firm, has agreed to pay $1,050,000 to settle apparent violations of OFAC sanctions targeting Russia's financial sector.
Between April 2019 and May 2021, FTI indirectly dealt in prohibited debt of VTB Bank OAO, a Russian state-owned bank on OFAC's Sectoral Sanctions Identification List, on six occasions.
The violations occurred when FTI extended debt of more than 14 days maturity to VTB by indirectly issuing invoices that went unpaid or were paid long past the permissible tenor.

articles.headline: Adani Enterprises Limited Settles for $275,000,000 Over Iranian-Origin Gas Shipments
body: Adani Enterprises Limited (AEL), an India-headquartered multinational company, has agreed to pay $275,000,000 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC sanctions on Iran.

From November 2023 to June 2025, AEL purchased shipments of liquified petroleum gas (LPG) from a Dubai-based trader, causing U.S. financial institutions to process 32 U.S. dollar payments totaling over $192 million for Iranian-origin LPG.
OFAC determined the violations were egregious and not voluntarily self-disclosed, noting that red flags should have put AEL on notice that the LPG originated from Iran.

articles.headline: TradeStation Securities, Inc. Fined $1,110,661 by OFAC
body: TradeStation Securities, Inc. has been assessed a civil penalty of $1,110,661 by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on March 17, 2026.
The specific details of the apparent violations leading to this penalty were not immediately disclosed.
This enforcement action highlights OFAC's continued vigilance in ensuring compliance with U.S. sanctions regulations across the financial services industry.

articles.headline: Individual Fined $3,777,000 by OFAC
body: An individual has been assessed a civil penalty of $3,777,000 by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on February 25, 2026.
The details of the apparent violations leading to this significant penalty were not immediately released.
This substantial fine underscores OFAC's commitment to holding individuals accountable for sanctions breaches, regardless of their affiliation with corporate entities.

articles.headline: IMG Academy, LLC Pays $1,720,000 for Counternarcotics Sanctions Violations
body: IMG Academy, LLC, a private boarding school and athletic training institution, has agreed to pay $1,720,000 to settle apparent violations of OFAC counternarcotics sanctions.

Over a five-year period, IMG Academy entered into tuition enrollment agreements and processed payments with two individuals designated under the Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Designation Act due to their ties to a sanctioned Mexican drug cartel.

OFAC found that IMG Academy failed to conduct basic screening or due diligence that would have identified the individuals as sanctioned, despite having full name details that matched entries on the SDN List.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.
